source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: The decision cycle has five phases: input, elaboration (rules propose and evaluate operators in parallel until quiescence), operator selection (a fixed decision procedure over preferences), application, output. Control is operator-centric. Knowledge lives in rules; a fixed procedure, not a learned judge, picks the operator.
numbers: Soar version 9.6. No experiment; architecture description.
quote: If the preferences are inconclusive or in conflict, then no operator is selected, and an impasse arises
limits: Overview paper, not an experiment. Elaboration order is not fixed; the waves are only a common pattern.
agent_relevance: Our schema already has code decide transitions (section 1). Soar shows the same split: cheap parallel proposal first, one fixed procedure decides, deliberation only if that fails.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Preferences are the data structure that decides selection. Acceptable preferences say an operator is available. Evaluative preferences say whether it should be chosen: better, worse, best, worst, reject, indifferent, and numeric (expected reward). Rules create them, and they retract when the rule's match goes away (truth maintenance).
numbers: Relative types: better, worse, equal; absolute: best, worst, reject; plus numeric. No rule counts.
quote: Acceptable preferences are created by operator proposal rules to indicate an operator is available for selection
limits: Retraction by truth maintenance means a proposal can vanish if the situation changes.
agent_relevance: Our O1-O8 operators are proposals. We could log them as acceptable, and keep check results as separate evaluative signals. That keeps proposing and judging apart (G5).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Three impasse classes, tied to three knowledge failures. State no-change: no operator proposed. Operator tie/conflict: several proposed, evaluation preferences insufficient or contradictory. Operator no-change: the same operator stays selected over several cycles (cannot apply it, or the action takes time outside). For slow external actions the usual response is just to wait.
numbers: Three classes here; the Manual splits tie and conflict and adds constraint-failure (see a09).
quote: Operator no-change: The same operator stays selected across multiple decision cycles.
limits: Operator no-change is ambiguous: missing knowledge or a slow external action. Soar needs rules to tell them apart.
agent_relevance: Maps to S6 triggers: no candidate (state no-change), several equal candidates or disagreeing checks (tie/conflict), same attempt retried with no pass in two rounds (operator no-change). Note the wait case: a slow tool call must not fire doubt (G1).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: On an impasse Soar makes a substate linked to the superstate. The substate has its own preference memory and can select and apply operators without disturbing the superstate. It sees superstate structures and has semantic and episodic memory, but not perception or motor; those go through the topstate so the outside world is monitored there. Impasses can stack. Changes the substate makes to the superstate are its results. The impasse is resolved when a decision is possible in the superstate; then the substate and all non-result structure is deleted.
numbers: Stack depth unbounded in principle; no numbers.
quote: When an impasse is resolved, the substate terminates and all non-result substate structures are automatically removed.
limits: Results that are elaborations in the superstate persist only while their support holds; results of an operator application do not retract.
agent_relevance: Supports the rule that a subgoal returns only its result. Also: the subagent must not touch the world directly; actions go through the parent (G2, G6). Cap stack depth and tokens (see a06).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Laird presents impasses as the single route to meta-reasoning. Instead of separate meta modules (he names MIDCA and Clarion), Soar reuses the same decision cycle recursively. Substate processing is metalevel deliberation (Newell's second cognitive level). Chunking later turns it into rules, so the higher level is replaced by rules with experience. He warns that a System 1 / System 2 mapping is overly simple.
numbers: Qualitative.
quote: this is essentially the philosophy of "going meta" when directly available knowledge is inadequate
limits: Design claim, not tested here against a separate-module design.
agent_relevance: Argues for one reflective mechanism triggered by typed failure, not many always-on critics. Matches G1.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Deliberate operator selection in a substate yields look-ahead search: imagine each operator's result with internal models, evaluate, repeat. Different search methods (iterative deepening, best-first, alpha-beta) arise from which knowledge is available. Deliberation costs time, so the substate can be time-monitored and a non-optimal or random decision made. A footnote says extra preferences can always remove a selection impasse, in the extreme by copying tied operators.
numbers: No timing numbers in this paper.
quote: There is a tradeoff in that deliberate reasoning in a substate takes more time.
limits: The time-bound fallback is mentioned, not specified or measured.
agent_relevance: Pattern: tie -> bounded lookahead -> fall back to a cheap pick when the budget runs out. Fits G6 (never abstain) and G7 (pay for itself). We need an explicit budget per impasse.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Chunking maps impasse type to learned rule type: state no-change -> operator proposal rules; tie/conflict -> operator evaluation rules (search control; numeric ones become RL rules); operator no-change -> operator application rules; any impasse -> elaborations. Chunking needs deterministic substate decisions and is not used when decisions rested on numeric preferences. Laird says chunk overhead is minimal in empirical results (Assanie 2022).
numbers: No overhead numbers in this paper; it cites Assanie (2022).
quote: chunking requires that substate decisions be deterministic so that they will always create the same result
limits: Overhead claim is cited, not shown. The determinism limit matters for noisy LLM judgments.
agent_relevance: Typed lessons for the S9 library: store a proposal heuristic after state no-change, an evaluation rule after tie, a procedure after operator no-change. Do not store lessons that rested on sampled or voted choices.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Reinforcement learning in Soar tunes operator selection only when the other, non-RL preferences are insufficient. Numeric preferences are the last tiebreaker, below rules and symbolic preferences.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Only the lines on this point were read closely.
agent_relevance: Order of authority: hard rules and checks first, learned value only to break remaining ties. Fits G5 (code selects).

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: Four impasse types come from the preference scheme. Tie: preferences do not separate two or more acceptable operators. Conflict: at least two operators have contradictory better/worse preferences and none is rejected, prohibited or required. Constraint-failure: more than one required value, or a value both required and prohibited. No-change: no new operator selected, split into state no-change and operator no-change.
numbers: Four types, five if no-change is split.
quote: There can be only one type of impasse at a given level of subgoaling at a time.
limits: Constraint-failure outranks tie and conflict: if both occur, only constraint-failure is detected.
agent_relevance: Our schema names only no-change and tie. Constraint-failure is a third case: two hard requirements that cannot both hold (for example two checks that demand different outputs). More preferences cannot fix it; only changing the constraints can. Candidate new trigger for S6.

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: Preference semantics: acceptable, reject, better/worse (partial order, no implicit transitivity), best, worst, unary and binary indifferent, require, prohibit. Selection is a fixed eight-step filter: RequireTest, AcceptableCollect, ProhibitFilter, RejectFilter, BetterWorseFilter, BestFilter, WorstFilter, IndifferentFilter. Five of the steps can exit with a winner or an impasse.
numbers: Eight steps, five exits.
quote: Only a single value can be selected as the current operator, that is, all values are mutually exclusive.
limits: The manual flags a quirk: a value better than a best value wins. Indifferent candidates are picked at random by default.
agent_relevance: An ordered, code-checkable arbitration. Our code can copy the shape: hard constraints, then drop rejected, then comparisons, then defaults, with an explicit impasse exit at each point (G5).

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: Where each impasse is raised: after the reject step an empty set gives no-change; after the better/worse filter an empty set gives conflict (every candidate lost to another); after best and worst filters an empty set gives no-change; the indifferent filter raises tie when candidates are not mutually indifferent. Require/prohibit clashes raise constraint-failure at the first step.
numbers: Exit points 1 to 4, plus the first and last step.
quote: If the set of remaining candidates is empty, a conflict impasse is created returning the set of all candidates passed into this filter
limits: Descriptive of 9.6; older versions differ.
agent_relevance: The impasse carries the candidate set and its cause. Our impasse record should too: which attempts, which evidence clashed. That feeds the subgoal prompt (G2).

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: How each impasse is resolved. Tie: add preferences that prefer one, remove others, or make all indifferent. Conflict: require one or reject/prohibit the others. Constraint-failure: not resolvable by more preferences; change rules so fewer require/prohibit preferences are made, or have the substate retract all but one conflicting preference. State no-change: create acceptable or require preferences for operators. Operator no-change: apply the operator, change the state so the proposal no longer matches, or prefer another operator.
numbers: Five resolution recipes.
quote: A constraint-failure impasse cannot be resolved by additional preferences
limits: Recipes say what resolves each type, not how often each works.
agent_relevance: A typed response table for S6: tie -> pick or compare; conflict -> reject one side by an outside check; no-change -> generate new candidates or reframe; constraint-failure -> relax the constraint (links to the constraint-relaxation subfield).

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: Resolved vs eliminated vs regenerated. Resolved: substate results let a new operator be chosen; Soar can learn. Eliminated: a higher impasse resolved, or the world changed so selection became possible; no learning. Regenerated: the substate's reasoning depended on superstate facts that changed, so it is thrown away and rebuilt; no learning. Soar tracks which superstate elements the substate reasoning used.
numbers: Qualitative. Example: a block thrown out of the window during blocks-world deliberation.
quote: the problem solving in the subgoal is inconsistent, and the state created in response to the original impasse is removed
limits: Dependency tracking is architectural; an LLM scaffold has none unless we build it.
agent_relevance: If the evidence a subgoal relied on changes (a check result is replaced, the problem is restated), discard the subgoal and learn nothing from it. Needs a dependency list per subgoal (G2).

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: Results of a subgoal are only the working memory elements and preferences linked to a superstate. Soar builds a temporary justification: conditions are the superstate elements the result needed, the action is the result. So the parent keeps the result with its reasons, not the substate scratch work. Each state has at most one substate; a stack of substates; all levels keep firing.
numbers: Qualitative.
quote: The results of a subgoal are the working memory elements and preferences that were created in the substate
limits: Negated conditions on substate-local items are dropped, which can make a justification over-general (the manual warns).
agent_relevance: Return from a subgoal: result plus the list of parent facts it depended on. That list lets the parent drop the result if those facts change, and later feeds the lesson store.

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.4 Procedural Knowledge Learning
finding: Chunking was redesigned (explanation-based behavior summarization). Old chunks were over-specific; new ones are far more general. Rules learned from tie impasses need the knowledge behind the operator preferences (relevant operator selection knowledge) or they can be wrong; this option is off by default. If the substate used random, numeric or RL selection, no rule is added at all.
numbers: In Soar 9.4 the arithmetic agent learned 1263 rules; in 9.6 the same agent learns 8.
quote: chunks created in such a problem space will not be correct
limits: One example agent for the 1263 to 8 figure; no benchmark.
agent_relevance: Boundary for the lesson store: a lesson learned from a tie settled by a sampled or voted pick is unsafe to store (G4). Also store the reason for the choice with the lesson.

source: Laird et al. (2017) Soar Manual 9.6, ch.2 The Soar Architecture
finding: Execution detail: proposal-phase effects are i-supported (they retract when their match disappears) and application effects are o-supported (persist until removed). A selected operator can be deselected between waves if its proposal retracts.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Soar implementation detail; no direct LLM counterpart.
agent_relevance: A thing proposed on evidence must be withdrawn when the evidence goes. Our attempt queue should drop candidates whose supporting check is later invalidated.

source: Laird (2021) An Analysis and Comparison of ACT-R and Soar
finding: In Soar, failures to propose, select or apply all become impasses, and the substate records the impasse type, giving 'module status data' that enables metacognitive reasoning. ACT-R has no automatic substate; a port would need an extra buffer holding impasse information, giving at least one level of metareasoning. The primitive deliberate act takes about 50 msec in human models.
numbers: About 50 ms per primitive deliberate act (human-modelling assumption).
quote: Soar's use of operators leads to impasse-driven subgoaling that supports metareasoning, planning, and other aspects of complex cognition
limits: Written by a Soar author. Whether one extra buffer suffices for rich metareasoning is stated as open.
agent_relevance: The rival architecture lacks impasse-driven subgoaling. The minimal useful part may be just the typed failure record plus a place to reason about it.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: CoALA describes Soar in a few lines (memories, decision loop, impasse -> subgoal) and then defines its own decision cycle: planning stage (propose, evaluate, select) then execution. Selection can reject all actions and loop back to proposal. CoALA keeps no typed impasse and no substate; the loop-back is the only trace of the idea.
numbers: Survey of many agents; no new experiment.
quote: If no actions are valid, or multiple actions tie, then an impasse occurs. Soar creates a subgoal to resolve the impasse
limits: Survey; CoALA does not measure whether typed impasses help.
agent_relevance: The main LLM-agent blueprint dropped the impasse typing. Our S6 would add what CoALA lacks: a named cause for failure and an isolated sub-run.

source: Sumers et al. (2024) CoALA, planning stage and case studies
finding: CoALA notes that early agents just propose one action; later work added reasoning and retrieval, and then iterative proposal and evaluation of several actions. Tree of Thoughts and RAP use LLMs for BFS/DFS and Monte Carlo tree search. In Soar terms this is look-ahead evaluation that Soar starts only after a tie, while the LLM agents run it at every step.
numbers: No quantities in this passage.
quote: Followup work has exploited intermediate reasoning and retrieval to analyze the situation, make and maintain action plans
limits: The contrast with Soar is mine, by description; CoALA does not measure it.
agent_relevance: Soar's lazy deliberation (only on impasse) versus always-on search is testable: same tokens, impasse-gated lookahead vs every-step lookahead (G1, G7). Not tested in CoALA.

source: NL2GenSym authors (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR
finding: An LLM generator writes Soar rules for the Water Jug Problem from natural language; an LLM critic reads Soar execution traces (decision cycles, impasses) and sends fix suggestions. The best solution of the two-jug case takes 5 decision cycles.
numbers: Cases include 30 hard (11-20 steps) and 20 three-jug variants; overall mean minimum cycles 7.97; baselines manual, zero-shot, one-shot; cap 500,000 decision cycles per case. Easy and medium counts not captured.
limits: Single toy domain. Only part of the dataset breakdown was read.
agent_relevance: Soar's own run trace (cycles, impasses) is a code-made signal a critic can read. Matches G2: revise from real execution output, not from opinion.

source: NL2GenSym authors (2025) NL2GenSym results
finding: With the framework, Gemini-2.5 flash reaches 86% success at about 1.76 times the minimum decision cycles; qwen-max reaches 91% at 1.98 times. One-shot reaches 55% (Gemini pro) and 66% (qwen). Zero-shot is 0%. Manual encoding gets 84% success but its cycles average over 1000 times the minimum.
numbers: Overall success: manual 84%, zero-shot 0%, one-shot 55% (Gemini) / 66% (qwen), framework 86% / 91%. Hard cases: manual 46.67%, one-shot Gemini 20%, framework 76.67% (Gemini) / 86.67% (qwen). The 1.98 figure belongs to qwen-max, not Gemini.
limits: Table read from extracted text and checked against the prose. One task family. Success means executable rules that reach the goal.
agent_relevance: A small model plus an execution-grounded critic beat a larger model without one (86% vs 55%). Supports G2/G7: the loop around real output is worth more than model size, here for symbolic rule writing.

source: NL2GenSym authors (2025) NL2GenSym ablation
finding: Removing the critic hurts most: success falls 23 points overall and 37 points on hard and variant cases, and average cycles exceed 1000 times the minimum. Removing the basic knowledge base costs 17 points; removing the case knowledge base costs 14 points.
numbers: -23 points (no critic), -17 (no basic KB), -14 (no case KB).
limits: One task; reported as percent reductions in the paper.
agent_relevance: The execution-feedback critic was the active ingredient, as in G2. Retrieval of prior cases (our lesson library) was worth about 14 points here.

source: NL2GenSym authors (2025) NL2GenSym critic feedback examples
finding: An appendix example critic message says the generated agent hit a state no-change impasse that led to an infinite loop, and asks for explicit handling of all five impasse types: state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict, constraint-failure. Hand-written baseline agents hit the 500,000-cycle cap on hard cases.
numbers: Cap 500,000 decision cycles; hard-case manual success 46.67%.
limits: One appendix example, not a systematic count of impasse types seen.
agent_relevance: Infinite state no-change loops are a real failure mode, so an impasse detector needs a loop guard. Our two-round no-pass rule plays this role.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing LLMs and Soar for Explainable Recommendation
finding: Design: a Soar agent runs; on an impasse (the example is a tie between two rules proposing different movies) a converter sends a structured query (profile, goal, candidates, impasse reason) to an LLM (DeepSeek-V3). The reply is parsed into condition-action text and compiled by chunking into a new rule. About 500 initial rules were bootstrapped by the LLM from about 10 prompt templates per dataset.
numbers: MovieLens-1M: 6,040 users, 3,416 items, 999,611 interactions. Amazon Movies: 123,960 users, 50,052 items. Yelp: 43,702 users, 51,068 items.
limits: Authors' own system. The example shows a tie impasse; results are not broken out by impasse type.
agent_relevance: The closest real build to impasse-gated LLM help. The query format (state, goal, candidates, impasse reason) is a ready template for our subgoal call.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec results and ablations
finding: CogRec reports the best scores on all three datasets. On MovieLens-1M HR@10 is 0.3124 against a second-best near 0.2956 (+5.7%); gains over second-best are 4.1 to 9.1 percent across the metric columns. Without chunking, results drift toward the LLM-only baseline and LLM call frequency stays high; with chunking it falls to a low plateau. Without LLM bootstrap, performance drops a lot.
numbers: HR@10 0.3124 on ML-1M; improvements 4.1% to 9.1%; LLM-Direct 0.2815 on ML-1M HR@10. Ablation values are in a figure only.
limits: Extracted table rows were scrambled, so which baseline is second-best is uncertain. Gains are small. No variance, seeds or significance tests. The pure Soar baseline is about 20 hand rules with no LLM.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence: small gains, no statistics. The clear qualitative result is that stored rules cut later LLM calls. Treat as a design example, not proof that impasse gating improves accuracy.

source: Kirk, Wray, Laird (2023) Exploiting Language Models as a Source of Knowledge for Cognitive Agents
finding: A Soar task-learning agent asks GPT-3 for goals in a tidy-kitchen task and checks each answer itself before use. Over 70% of the responses were not viable for the embodied agent; only a small share were situationally relevant.
numbers: 35 kitchen objects; over 70% of LLM responses unviable (human-coded classes: unviable, viable but unreasonable, reasonable, situationally relevant).
limits: Position paper with early results; GPT-3, one task. The chart gives the shares; text gives only over 70%.
agent_relevance: Answers from an LLM entering a subgoal need an outside viability check before returning as results (G2, G3). Most raw answers would have been wrong for the agent.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: STARS lets the agent analyse and repair LLM goal descriptions with its own knowledge, then select. Without human oversight, task completion rises from 52.5% / 66.7% / 35.7% (template prompting baseline) to 77.5% / 94.4% / 92.9% for tidy kitchen / store groceries / organize office. With oversight, user words fall by 52 to 68%. A search tree alone gave no gain but is a prerequisite for the analysis-and-repair step.
numbers: 58 unique objects over three tasks (35 kitchen, 12 office; groceries by subtraction 11). Completion 52.5->77.5, 66.7->94.4, 35.7->92.9. With missing context added: 92.5% on tidy kitchen. Unviable raw responses: 70%+ (kitchen), 58% (groceries), 85% (office).
limits: The agent is a Soar agent, but the paper has no dedicated impasse mechanism; the LLM is called when a goal is unknown. Simulated tasks, task-specific agent.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G3: checking and repairing answers from real task knowledge raised completion by 25 to 57 points. More candidates without a check (search tree) gave nothing, matching G4.

source: Mohan, Mininger, Kirk, Laird (2012) Acquiring Grounded Representations of Words with Situated Interactive Instruction
finding: A Soar agent turns each failure to ground a word or run a command into an impasse and starts a new instructor interaction to fill the gap; it handles several failures one at a time. Learning is fast: colors 100% after about 1 example per color; sizes 100% after 1.5 per size; shapes 96% after 12.9 per shape; spatial prepositions 93.98% of 144 arrangements after 3.17 examples per preposition; new action verbs converged after 1.26 examples per command and all tests ran correctly.
numbers: Averages over three runs; 12 objects per property, 6 prepositions, 144 arrangements; one verb template had 64 instantiations and two examples were enough.
limits: Small closed domain, Soar-specific; evaluation done by an outside firm. No comparison with a non-impasse agent.
agent_relevance: An impasse can mean 'ask the right source for what is missing'. For us the source may be the user, a tool or a check, not only the model. The impasse type says what to ask for.

source: Fan and Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: After coding 42 modern agent systems against ten historical architectures, the authors find the Soar bundle, typed impasse plus isolated substate plus compiling the resolution into a reusable rule, is still not delivered by any reviewed system. PALADIN and AgentDebugX give typed failure; Shepherd gives a reversible branch; Reflexion and AgentHER give failure learning; none couples them with a typed return and safe reuse conditions.
numbers: 10 architectures, 8 runtime families, 42 systems; evidence grades E1-E4, depth D0-D4; Soar-linked parts coded E2/D3 to E3/D4.
quote: Soar's stronger chain couples a typed impasse to a protected substate, returns a typed resolution
limits: Two authors' own coding (2026). Absence is relative to their search.
agent_relevance: The gap is real and, per this review, unmeasured: no published LLM system tested typed-impasse subgoaling as a whole. A test of ours would be new. Also lists near systems for other subfields.

source: Wray, Kirk, Laird (2021) Language Models as a Knowledge Source for Cognitive Agents
finding: Review of how a cognitive agent could use a language model as a knowledge source. It names accuracy and relevance as the two most significant challenges and says the agent should check what it gets.
numbers: Abstract and challenge section only.
quote: The issues of Accuracy and Relevance are probably the most significant challenges.
limits: Only the abstract and a few passages were read; position paper.
agent_relevance: Motivates agent-side checks on any model answer returned from a subgoal.

source: Allen (1988) Production System Chunking in Soar: Case Studies in Automated Learning (NASA JSC report)
finding: A short secondary report states the early Soar design: universal subgoaling means that when a stage lacks information a subgoal is created to collect it and pushed on a goal stack; when the information is available the subgoal pops. Listed traits: problem spaces, universal subgoaling to resolve impasses, and no conflict-resolution mechanism.
numbers: Soar then about 255 KB of Lisp plus 100 KB of modified OPS5.
quote: there is no conflict resolution mechanism in SOAR
limits: Secondary, short, poor OCR; not a primary source.
agent_relevance: The design refused to settle ambiguity with a fixed rule and spent effort only when ambiguity arose, which is our G1.

source: Laird, Newell, Rosenbloom (1987) SOAR: An architecture for general intelligence
finding: Founding paper (Artificial Intelligence 33:1-64). Search summaries name universal subgoaling (any decision can be the object of goal-oriented attention) and automatic subgoaling (goals arise only from impasses).
numbers: Not read: the DTIC server returned a block page to every download this session.
limits: Source not opened; claims come from search-result summaries and Laird 2022 citations.
agent_relevance: Primary source still to read for original task results (weak methods emerging from impasses, eight-puzzle) with numbers.

source: Laird (2012) The Soar Cognitive Architecture (MIT Press)
finding: The Soar book: decision cycle, preferences, impasse types, substates, chunking, RL, memories. Laird 2022 says it supplements this book for depth.
numbers: Not opened (book; no open copy found).
limits: Not read. Soar content in this file comes from Laird 2022 and the Manual.
agent_relevance: Needed for the rationale of the preference scheme and long-running application numbers.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: the anatomy of a general learning mechanism
finding: Classic chunking paper (Machine Learning 1:11-46): learning from subgoal results, with a demonstration of macro-operator acquisition.
numbers: Not opened; DTIC copy returned a block page. No eight-puzzle speedups were found in any opened source.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Owned by the chunking subfield; listed so that agent can fill in numbers.

source: Nason and Laird (2005) Soar-RL: Integrating reinforcement learning with Soar
finding: Numeric preferences updated by reward, used only when symbolic preferences leave a tie. Described in Laird 2022 section 5.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not read; the link to impasses is taken from Laird 2022.
agent_relevance: Possible base for scoring subgoal strategies by past success (S0 class record).
